### Constitutional Challenge to Sub-section (4) of Section 8

The constitutional challenge to sub-section (4) of Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is that it is **ultra vires the Constitution** [Case: LILY THOMAS vs UNION OF INDIA . | No Citation | Supreme Court of India, 2013]. This means the provision is being challenged on the grounds that it is unconstitutional and beyond the legislative power of Parliament.

### Specific Protection Provided to Sitting Legislators

Sub-section (4) of Section 8 provides a specific protection to sitting legislators (members of Parliament or State Legislatures) who are convicted of certain offences. The protection is as follows:

If a sitting legislator files an appeal or revision against their conviction within three months, the disqualification that would otherwise result from the conviction **will not take effect immediately**. Instead, the disqualification is postponed and will only take effect if and when the appeal or revision is finally decided by the appropriate court [Case: LILY THOMAS vs UNION OF INDIA . | No Citation | Supreme Court of India, 2013].
reference: The constitutional challenge to sub-section (4) of Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 is that it is ultra vires the Constitution. The specific protection it provides to sitting legislators is that notwithstanding anything in sub-sections (1), (2) or (3) of Section 8, a disqualification under either subsection shall not, in the case of a person who on the date of the conviction is a member of Parliament or the Legislature of a State, take effect until three months have elapsed from that date or, if within that period an appeal or application for revision is brought in respect of the conviction or the sentence, until that appeal or application is disposed of by the court.

Based on the provided context, when a husband is sentenced to imprisonment for non-payment of maintenance arrears under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, this imprisonment does **not** constitute satisfaction of the maintenance liability. Actual payment of the arrears remains necessary for the order to be considered satisfied.

The Supreme Court has explicitly distinguished between the mode of enforcement and the mode of satisfaction of a maintenance order.

**Key Legal Principle:**

The Supreme Court in **[Case: BEGUM SUBANU ALIAS SAIRA BANU & ANR. vs A.M. ABDUL GAFOOR | No Citation | Supreme Court of India, 1987]** held:

> "Distinction to be made between mode of enforcement and mode of satisfaction of maintenance order-Sentencing the person to jail is a mode of enforcement and not a mode of satisfaction of the liability."

The Court further clarified:

> "Actual payment must be made for satisfaction of the order."

**Supporting Case Law:**

This principle is illustrated by the facts of the case **[Case: SMT. KULDIP KAUR vs SURINDER SINGH AND ANR. | No Citation | Supreme Court of India, 1988]**. In this case, the Metropolitan Magistrate had rejected the wife's application for recovery of maintenance arrears on the ground that the husband's imprisonment for one month had satisfied the claim. The Supreme Court took up the appeal against this decision, indicating that the magistrate's view was incorrect. The case underscores that imprisonment is a coercive measure to compel payment, but it does not extinguish the debt itself.

In summary, imprisonment is a tool for enforcing the court's order, but the liability to pay the maintenance amount continues until the arrears are actually paid to the person entitled to receive them.
reference: Under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, when a husband is sentenced to imprisonment for non-payment of maintenance arrears, this imprisonment does not constitute satisfaction of the maintenance liability. The Supreme Court has clearly distinguished between 'mode of enforcement' and 'mode of satisfaction' of the liability. Sentencing a person to jail is a 'mode of enforcement' and not a 'mode of satisfaction' of the liability. The liability can be satisfied only by making actual payment of the arrears. The purpose of sending a person to jail is to oblige them to comply with the order and make the payment, not to wipe out the liability which they have refused to discharge. A sentence of jail is no substitute for the recovery of the amount of monthly allowance which has fallen in arrears.
